items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, maybe it was more of Billy Strayhorn, you know it’s so hard to kind of separate one from the other, but the “Daybreak Express,” 1932 I think. And I think it was 1958, “Track 360,” that’s an amazing work, one minute.

ctx.x: The farm workers, yeah. That’s actually a bit less specific, but, yeah, the farm workers. Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, maybe it was more of Billy Strayhorn, you know it’s so hard to kind of separate one from the other, but the “Daybreak Express,” 1932 I think. And I think it was 1958, “Track 360,” that’s an amazing work, one minute. I think it’s one minute or two minutes long. And then, well, Steve Reich’s “Different Trains” in 1988, for string quartet and recordings. So I immersed myself in all this…

You had mentioned in the interview from ten years ago, it’s a bit of a paraphrase here, but you said that the Chinese are not ready for what I’m offering. And I wasn’t quite sure if you were talking about Chinese-Americans or that you were trying to see if you could get your music played in China. Do you remember? And is it still the case?

items.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: it’s from my study of music of Wayne Shorter and Billy Strayhorn in terms of how they use color and timbre

ctx.x: David is, yeah, he’s just, I can’t say that — he’s just on an amazing high level. And just my brief experience of us working together just elevated me on a level. And he’s just very generous and patient. And last year I was commissioned by the Rockefeller Multi- Arts Production Fund, the San Francisco Arts Commission and Meet the Composer in New York to compose a work called “Up From the Root” which was to celebrate Chinese-American identity, Chinese diaspora specifically. Because I’d attended a conference where…

called “Sweet Whisper of a Flower” that I composed. And it has — I hate to use the word influences — but it’s from my study of music of Wayne Shorter and Billy Strayhorn in terms of how they use color and timbre. And so what I did was I took a Chinese melody like the “Golden Snake Dance,” and put in a different tempo that was more like a ballad impressionistic. And then I wrote a countermelody that had characteristics of a Chinese folk melody but placed in different beats, places, accents, so that it would be…
That defining swing is always a hard thing to do. Are there words that you can use? Or is it more of a trying to show them with your instrument?
